transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hey, yeah. Uh, so what brought me in is... I guess things just got really intense lately. Like, I'm usually just a normal crew guy, right? Landscaping. Mowing, edging, laying down mulch. 

Actually, the mulch we got this season was complete garbage. It was supposed to be premium cedar, but it came off the truck smelling like absolute swamp water, and I told my boss, Dave, I was like, "Dave, we can't put this in the Johnson's yard, they'll have a fit." They're these clients over on Westside who complained last year because a single dandelion grew near their mailbox. People are crazy about their lawns, man. I mean, I get wanting it to look nice, but you live outside, nature is gonna happen. 

But, uh... wait, what was I saying? Oh, right. Why I'm here. Yeah, so I went from just being a regular guy doing the heavy lifting to suddenly trying to run three massive commercial bids all by myself. I was calling city people, trying to line up all these wholesale plant suppliers... I started messaging everybody I knew, like everyone in my phone, about this giant community park idea I had. It was like a switch flipped and I just couldn't shut it off, you know?
Can you tell me if there was a specific time when you felt unusually energetic, more confident, or unusually irritable, where your thoughts and actions seemed to speed up significantly?

Yeah, exactly. Before I crashed, I was just... I felt so fired up. Like I was almost bigger than myself, you know? Unstoppable. Which is funny because I'm not a huge guy, but I felt like I could uproot a stump with my bare hands. 

Speaking of trees, we were supposed to put in this huge row of Green Giant arborvitaes for a privacy screen a few weeks ago. Those things grow crazy fast, like three feet a year if you water them right. But you gotta make sure the root flare is exposed when you plant them or they just suffocate in the dirt. People always bury them way too deep, like they're sinking a fence post. My uncle Rick did that to his Japanese maple and I told him, I said, "Rick, you're choking the poor thing," but he never listens. He's so stubborn. He thinks he's an expert because he watched one YouTube video on pruning, but he completely butchered his hydrangeas last spring. Just chopped them to the ground. 

But, uh... wait. What were we talking about? Oh, right, the energy thing. Yeah. So I had all this energy and these big plans, and if any of the guys on the crew questioned my plan or told me to slow down—especially Tommy, who takes a twenty-minute smoke break every hour anyway—I would just snap at him. Like, way harder than made any sense. I'd just completely bite his head off if he even looked at me wrong.
Can you describe how long you felt that way — that fired up, unstoppable, with so much energy and so many plans?

Well, that whole fired-up stretch... it really kicked off right when I started remaking myself for that park pitch I mentioned. I was getting everything ready, you know? I even went out and bought all these new clipboards and, like, high-end polo shirts so I'd look like a real project manager when I met with the city. 

And I was at the hardware store every morning right when they opened at 6 AM. Man, the guys at the Pro Desk know me by name now. Especially Carl. Carl's a good dude, he used to do hardscaping over in Springfield before he blew out his knee. It's always the knees or the lower back in this job. You gotta lift with your legs, but nobody actually does that when you're wrestling a 200-pound root ball out of a truck bed. We had this one guy on the crew, Gary, who tried to macho a boulder by himself last summer and he was out for a whole season. Workers comp is a nightmare for small businesses, my boss Dave complains about the insurance premiums non-stop. He says if one more guy gets hurt, he's just gonna sell the trucks and retire to Florida. Which, I mean, you can't really blame him, the humidity down there is good for your joints, or so I hear. I've never been.

But... wait, sorry. I'm doing it again. What did you ask me? Oh, how long it went on. Right. Yeah, so that whole overconfident, unstoppable feeling... it lasted about two weeks. Two solid weeks of just running on pure rocket fuel before I completely crashed.
In that two-week period you described as being 'fired up,' did you feel that your mood was consistently elevated, unusually irritable, or both, almost every day for most of the day?

Yeah, it was pretty much all day, every day for those two weeks. Like I said, I just felt so fired up, like I was almost bigger than myself. Just completely on top of the world. 

But if anybody got in my way, man, it was bad. Like, if one of the guys questioned my plan or told me I needed to slow down, I would just snap at him. Way harder than made any sense. It's like I couldn't tolerate anyone not being on my exact wavelength. 

Which is weird, because usually I'm a pretty laid-back guy. Like, you have to be in landscaping, because things always go wrong. The weather changes, the equipment breaks down. Just last month, the starter on our main zero-turn mower went out, and we had to use the push mowers for three huge properties. It was miserable. My legs felt like jelly by the end of the day. But usually, I just roll with it, you know? You just get the job done. 

But during those two weeks... man, I was just so on edge. If Tommy even looked at me wrong, I'd bite his head off. It was like I had this engine revving inside me all the time, and any little bump in the road just made me explode.

During that two-week period when you felt so fired up and unstoppable, did you find yourself engaging in a lot more projects or activities than usual — like starting a bunch of new plans or pushing to get a lot more done than normal — even if others thought it was too much?

Yeah, definitely. I was just... I was taking on everything. I'd be up before daylight, loading all the tools into the truck, sketching out these massive new flower beds, pricing out all these native plants online. And then, even after a full day outside doing heavy labor, I still felt like I had to keep going. Like I couldn't stop moving. 

Speaking of native plants, it's actually super important to use them because they require way less water once they're established. People always want these crazy exotic things, like Bird of Paradise or whatever, but we live in a totally different climate zone. My neighbor, Mrs. Higgins, she planted all these tropicals on her patio and then was shocked—just completely shocked—when the first frost killed them all. I tried to tell her. I said, "Mrs. Higgins, those aren't gonna make it past October," but she just loved the colors. She's a nice lady, though. She always brings out lemonade when we're working nearby. Real lemonade, too, not that powdered stuff. Her grandson is actually trying to start a landscaping business too, but he doesn't know the first thing about soil pH. You gotta test the soil, or you're just throwing money away. 

But, uh, what was the question? Oh, right, doing more projects. Yeah, so I was just constantly going. Up before the sun, working all day, planning more stuff at night. I just felt like I had to do it all.

latest_inference.note: The patient described a distinct period of abnormally elevated mood, increased energy, and goal-directed activity lasting for two weeks, with irritability and marked functional impairment. This rules out F31.1 (Bipolar I disorder, current episode hypomanic) because the episode was not hypomanic but rather full manic (F31.2).

This episode involved goal-directed activity, grandiosity, and pressured speech, which supports the presence of a manic or hypomanic episode. However, without clarity on whether this episode caused marked impairment (versus merely being followed by a crash) or if there has been a prior depressive episode, the diagnosis remains unspecified within the bipolar spectrum.

The patient reported a distinct period of abnormally elevated and irritable mood lasting for at least two weeks, with increased goal-directed activity, decreased need for sleep, and impaired social or occupational functioning. This rules out F31.9 (bipolar disorder, unspecified) as the duration and severity of symptoms allow for a more specific diagnosis.
